strengths: Novel and intuitive framework that combines editable 3D convex primitive decomposition with a pretrained depth-conditioned rectified flow model, enabling semantically meaningful camera and object edits in images.

Effective texture hint generation via point cloud correspondences that projects source texture onto the edited view, improving identity preservation over key-value caching approaches such as StableFlow.
Variable primitive abstraction (e.g., K=4 to 72) gives users coarse-to-fine control, and the method does not require fine-tuning the depth-to-image generator.
Qualitative results are compelling, showing object translation, scaling, removal, camera moves, and compositional edits with strong texture retention.

Quantitative comparison with LooseControl shows substantially better geometric adherence (AbsRel) and texture consistency (PSNR/SSIM), and Table 2 validates depth approximation quality across primitive counts.
Clear writing, pipeline figures, algorithm details, hyperparameters, and failure-case discussion support reproducibility and honest positioning.
weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation is limited to essentially one baseline (LooseControl) and one main table, despite claims of outperforming prior works. Recent relevant methods such as DragDiffusion, StableFlow, Image Sculpting, and Obj3DiT are compared only qualitatively or not at all quantitatively.
No user study or human evaluation is provided for an interactive editing system, making it difficult to assess perceived editability, precision, and user preference.

The evaluation metrics (depth AbsRel and cycle-consistency PSNR/SSIM) may not reliably measure perceptual quality, identity preservation, or text alignment; they are also sensitive to the depth estimator and generative model used.

Ablations are mostly qualitative. There is no quantitative ablation isolating the texture hint, the confidence mask, primitive count effect on edit quality, or the contribution of the convex decomposition versus the FLUX depth conditioner.

The core technical novelty is partly an integration of existing components (CDIS-style convex decomposition and pretrained depth-conditioned FLUX), with the texture hint being a fairly straightforward reprojection and inpainting routine.

Reproducibility and scalability concerns remain: primitive predictors are trained separately for each K on 1.8M LAION images with pseudo-depth supervision, and automatic K selection via ensembling is not thoroughly validated.

Several important limitations are acknowledged but unresolved: failure on holes/occlusions, illumination and reflection inconsistencies, large object rotations, real-image inversion, and text-prompt conflicts that can produce artifacts.

strengths: Interesting and intuitive interface: editable 3D convex primitives provide a structured, selectable, and variable-resolution representation for image editing.
The pipeline creatively couples pretrained convex decomposition with a depth-conditioned rectified flow model (FLUX) and a training-free texture-hint mechanism.
The point-cloud correspondence and confidence mask idea is simple and appears effective for preserving object identity in several qualitative examples, including camera moves and object relocations.
The method supports multiple edit types (translation, scaling, deletion, camera motion) and variable primitive counts, enabling coarse-to-fine control.
Qualitative figures demonstrate plausible results on challenging edits, and the authors include a failure-case discussion.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the work largely combines existing components—CVXNet/CDIS-style convex primitive fitting, depth-conditioned FLUX, and warping/inpainting-based texture hints—without substantial technical innovation in generative modeling, primitive learning, or 3D editing.

Evaluation is far too narrow for the central claim of outperforming prior work: quantitative comparison is only against LooseControl on 48 images, with no comparisons to StableFlow, DragDiffusion, DiffusionHandles, Image Sculpting, OMG3D, Build-A-Scene, Obj3DiT, or other relevant 3D/object-editing baselines.

The proposed metrics are self-designed and potentially circular: geometry is evaluated using a depth estimator, and texture consistency uses the same point-cloud correspondence pipeline that generates the hint, which may favor the proposed method.

The claim of 'extensive evaluation' is unsupported; ablations are largely qualitative (Fig. 6), and there is no rigorous component-wise ablation of primitive decomposition, texture hint, confidence mask, number of primitives, or timestep range.

Reproducibility is weak: no code, models, or checkpoints are released; training details for the primitive predictor (losses, data filtering, optimization, camera calibration) are incomplete despite training on 1.8M LAION images.

The method relies heavily on pseudo-depth from DepthAnythingv2 and inferred camera intrinsics; no sensitivity analysis is provided for depth errors, focal-length errors, or in-the-wild camera calibration.

The comparison to LooseControl may be unfair or misconfigured, especially because LooseControl was designed for box-like primitives and the reported PSNR for it is extremely low (6.65), raising questions about baseline tuning.

Important failure modes are acknowledged but not solved: reflections/shadows do not move with objects, large rotations fail, cluttered scenes and holes are problematic, and the method does not handle view-dependent lighting or video consistency.
The evaluation lacks user studies, statistical significance, confidence intervals, or perceptual metrics, making it hard to judge practical editability and fidelity.

Positioning and claims are overbroad relative to evidence: the paper claims accurate camera moves, identity preservation, and composition generalization, but the experiments do not isolate these factors or test them at scale.
Ethical and societal implications of controllable image manipulation are not discussed.

Method exposition has gaps: the reverse diffusion and hint-injection equations are generic, hyperparameter selection is unclear, and algorithmic details for primitive extraction/refinement are relegated to prior work.

strengths: Introduces a novel and intuitive controllable image-editing framework that represents scenes as editable convex 3D primitives, supporting object moves, camera moves, scaling, deletion, and coarse-to-fine control via varying primitive counts.

Integrates primitive-based geometry with a pretrained depth-conditioned FLUX model and proposes a point-cloud correspondence-based texture hint with confidence masking, enabling texture/identity preservation without fine-tuning the generator.

Provides substantial qualitative evidence across several editing scenarios and compares against relevant baselines such as DragDiffusion, LooseControl, and StableFlow, including informative ablations and failure cases.
Reports quantitative improvements over LooseControl in geometric adherence and texture consistency, and offers implementation details, algorithms, and hyperparameter choices that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The main quantitative evaluation is limited to a single baseline (LooseControl); no numerical comparisons are provided against other relevant editing or 3D-aware manipulation methods such as DragDiffusion, Image Sculpting, Diffusion Self-Guidance, Object 3DIT, or OMG3D.

The proposed metrics have a circularity concern: texture PSNR/SSIM warps the edited image back using the method’s own correspondence pipeline, and depth AbsRel compares the input primitive depth to the estimated depth of an output that is explicitly conditioned on that depth, so high scores may not independently validate editability.
There is no human perceptual study or user evaluation despite the paper's emphasis on visual fidelity, editability, and identity preservation; this weakens support for the central claims.

Reproducibility remains limited: the method depends on large-scale training with LAION and several pretrained components, and the manuscript does not clearly specify model/code release, full prompts, or all training details for the primitive predictors.

Several important failure modes remain unresolved, including primitive decomposition failures in cluttered scenes, lighting/reflection and shadow inconsistencies, significant object rotations, depth-of-field/bokeh limitations, and conflicts between edits and the text prompt.
Ethical considerations and broader-impact safeguards for a powerful image-editing system are not discussed.

strengths: Introduces an intuitive 3D primitive-based image editing pipeline that supports object-level and part-level edits, camera moves, and variable levels of abstraction.

The texture hint generation via point-cloud correspondence and confidence masking effectively preserves source texture and object identity, with clear improvements over key-value transfer/StableFlow and no-hint baselines.

Demonstrates that existing pretrained depth-conditioned diffusion models, such as FLUX.1 Depth, can be steered by primitive-derived depth maps without additional fine-tuning, making the approach practical.

Provides strong quantitative evidence on depth adherence and texture consistency compared with LooseControl, along with helpful ablations on hint usage, StableFlow, timestep ranges, and LoRA depth weight.
Extensive qualitative examples, appendix algorithms, and implementation details support the claims and make the pipeline relatively reproducible.
weaknesses: The core technical components are largely incremental: convex primitive decomposition is borrowed from prior work, and the texture hint is essentially forward warping plus inpainting/confidence masking.

Evaluation is somewhat limited: the main quantitative table uses only 48 images and DragBench, with no user study and no comparison to several relevant 3D-aware editing methods such as Image Sculpting, OMG3D, Build-A-Scene, or FlowDrag.

The method relies on monocular depth and pseudo-depth supervision, with no true ground-truth 3D or camera poses; camera moves and geometry are therefore approximate, and the evaluation reuses the same depth/correspondence machinery, risking self-consistency bias.

Primitive decompositions are not guaranteed to align with semantic objects or parts, so users may need to manually select primitives, choose the number of primitives, tune mask dilation, timesteps, and LoRA weight, limiting fully automatic editability.
Acknowledged limitations remain unresolved, including non-convex shapes, significant rotations, reflections, view-dependent effects, depth-of-field, and temporal consistency for video.
The paper does not discuss broader ethical implications or potential misuse of image editing technology.

strengths: The paper presents an intuitive and visually compelling 3D primitive-based editing interface that supports object moves, part-level edits, camera moves, and variable levels of abstraction.

The integration of convex primitive decomposition with a depth-conditioned rectified flow model is technically reasonable, and the texture-hint/confidence-mask mechanism is a sensible way to improve identity preservation.
The authors provide substantial implementation detail, including hyperparameters, algorithms, and ablations, which helps clarify the pipeline.

The qualitative results and several ablations show that the proposed hint mechanism and primitive conditioning can improve geometry adherence and texture preservation relative to key-value transfer and LooseControl in the presented examples.
The paper is generally well-written and the high-level motivation for explicit 3D abstractions in image editing is clear.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is incremental: the approach largely combines existing components—convex decomposition from Vavilala et al. (2025a), DepthAnythingv2, FLUX depth-to-image, and StableFlow-style key-value transfer—with a projection-based texture hint that resembles standard 3D warping/novel-view synthesis adapted to diffusion models.

The evaluation is not sufficiently comprehensive for a top-tier claim. The main quantitative table compares only against LooseControl, while many directly relevant 3D-aware and drag-based editing methods (e.g., Image Sculpting, OMG3D, DragIn3D, FlowDrag, GoodDrag, Diffusion Handles, etc.) are not quantitatively compared.

The main comparison to LooseControl is potentially confounded because the authors supply their own primitives to both methods, even though LooseControl was not designed around this primitive extraction pipeline.

The texture-consistency metric is potentially circular: it uses the same point-cloud correspondence algorithm that is part of the proposed method to warp the synthesized image back for PSNR/SSIM evaluation, and the confidence mask filters out uncertain regions. This can overstate texture preservation and does not constitute an independent evaluation.

Depth accuracy is measured using DepthAnythingv2 as a pseudo-ground-truth depth estimator, not actual ground truth. The reliability of this metric on synthesized/edited images is questionable and is not thoroughly validated.

The paper claims superior visual fidelity, editability, and compositional generalization, but the evidence is mostly qualitative and small-scale (e.g., 48 test images in Table 1). There is no user study, edit-success rate, or systematic evaluation of compositional edits.

Failure modes are acknowledged qualitatively (non-convex shapes, significant rotations, view-dependent lighting, prompt conflicts), but they are not quantified or analyzed systematically, leaving the practical robustness of the method unclear.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or model release is mentioned, and the pipeline depends on complex external models and pseudo-labeled large-scale training data. The paper also does not discuss ethical/social implications of generative image editing.

Some central claims are stronger than the evidence: for example, 'extensive evaluation' is overstated given the limited baselines and metrics, and the 'training-free' framing omits that primitive extraction relies on trained networks and pseudo-depth supervision.

strengths: Introduces a novel interactive image editing paradigm using editable 3D convex primitives, enabling intuitive object-level and part-level manipulation, camera moves, and variable level-of-detail control.

Combines convex primitive decomposition with a depth-conditioned rectified flow model (FLUX) and a point-cloud-based texture-hint mechanism that preserves object identity and texture across edits, including handling occlusions via confidence masks.

Provides a substantial qualitative and quantitative evaluation, including comparisons to LooseControl, DragDiffusion, StableFlow, and production systems, along with ablations on primitive count, hint timesteps, LoRA weight, and mask dilation.

Demonstrates clear advantages over point-based drag editing and box-based layout control, particularly for maintaining perspective, scale, occlusion, and texture consistency across object and camera edits.

The image generation stage is training-free with respect to the diffusion model, making the method practical, and the primitive extraction is efficient enough for interactive use (1-3 seconds per image).
weaknesses: Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the method builds on existing convex decomposition (Vavilala et al., 2025a), a pretrained depth-conditioned FLUX model, and projection-based texture hinting; the core generative component is off-the-shelf.

Evaluation independence is limited: the main geometric metric uses DepthAnythingv2 to estimate depth of generated images, which may be biased when the generator is conditioned on primitive depth; texture consistency uses the same point cloud correspondence pipeline used for hint generation, potentially favoring the proposed method.

Baseline comparisons are not exhaustive for a top-tier venue: quantitative comparisons omit several relevant 3D-aware editing methods (e.g., Image Sculpting, OMG3D, DragIn3D), and key results use a small test set (48 images in Table 1).

Reproducibility is unclear: no code release or model weights are mentioned; primitive predictor training details (LAION subset, depth model, fitting procedure) and hyperparameters are only partially described, making independent replication difficult.

The method has several acknowledged limitations that may restrict practical use, including failures on non-convex shapes, rotations, reflections, view-dependent lighting, and conflicts with text prompts; hint timesteps and confidence-mask dilation appear sensitive.
Broader ethical implications and potential misuse for image manipulation/deepfakes are not discussed, which is increasingly expected at top-tier AI venues.
